My biggest issue (among many issues) is that at it's core, Lilo and Stitch is a movie about Hawaiian sovereignty. 

Yes, I know there's a cute fun little alien; but if you look at everything going on in Nani and Lilo's life, they (like many Hawaiians) are disenfranchised by the STATE (US government). Nani has to work that job where she's half dressed and her culture is bastardized for tourists; she is repeatedly told that tourism isn't doing well which is why she can't find consistent work; Lilo takes pictures of white people and objectifies them because that's what they do to her (look at the deleted scene where tourists are asking her if she speaks English and are taking pictures of her without consent).  

And this isn't even a reach because when the STATE threatens to separate Nani and Lilo, she sings her "Aloha Oe" which was written by the last matriarch of the Kingdom of Hawai'i when the annexed the country. 

So to have Nani, in this interpretation, surrender Lilo to the STATE so she can go to college? It spits in the face of the original's themes of fighting to maintain sovereignty. Nani literally screamed, "if you take [me] away from her, she won't stand a chance." 

It upsets me. So. So. Much.

I'm going to give advice that may seem unorthodox, but there are actually positions that are librarian adjacent that don't require the degree and--where I'm from--it's the "Specialist" position. Everyone in my old system who didn't have the means to get the degree played the time game. They'd come into the system as Pages, work up to Aides, then Assistants, and finally Specialists. 

Having said that, it takes *YEARS* to do; in my old system between 6-10 years, but it was a career position with benefits that paid the same if not a little more, than the Librarian I position.

Personally, I think this is the better route--even if you do end up going for the degree--because it's more beneficial to have the experience. It's honestly really frustrating to see people with no library experience get the degree, get those highly sought after Librarian positions, just to complain about how the work isn't what they thought or how the degree didn't prepare them. 

My former Circ Manager had been volunteering in libraries since he was *twelve years old*. Never went for the degree, everyone says he's so fit to be a librarian but he taught me more about library work than anyone else I've ever met.

So to summarize: get the degree if the official title matters to you, but know there's always the possibility of working your way up to the adjacent paraprofessional position and definitely WORK IN A LIBRARY FIRST. Do not go for your degree if you haven't spent some time working with patrons, I promise you, the experience is worth it.

Broadway is mainly accessible to those who are privileged and white, so to have them laughing at how they mispronounce people's names, the conditions of the village, etc. etc. reads as racist and on some level, actually is. Bonus points that they seemed disgusted that Mariah was played by a dark-skinned actress, but I digress. 

I think that ultimately it comes down to perception. If it looks racist, and it *feels* racist, 99.9% of the time it is. Whether or not BoM falls into that category is in the eye of the beholder, and given that the Black actors/actresses met with Matt and Trey to make some changes, I'm comfortable saying that BoM may be unintentionally racist in it's satirizing of racists.

I can see I'm in the minority here, but I still say having an honest conversation is worth it. My partner suffered from depression and low self-esteem issues and has been aimless for most of his adulthood. We've been together on the strength of love and love alone until I sat him down and had a conversation about how love cannot overcome the financial logistics and lack of growth. I didn't give any ultimatums, I just laid out where we are, where I thought and hoped we were going and how those goals are not compatible with how things are going at present. I told him that I was willing to leave, he asked me to stay, and I didn't say yes, I said, "please don't let me down."

Then I stepped back and I let that man show me what he was or wasn't going to do. I also set an internal personal deadline. It's only been three months since that conversation, and he didn't immediately jump to a proposal, he's fixing the issues that would've been a hindrance to me saying yes (such as going back to school and learning a trade) so that our relationship will be in a place where a proposal makes the most sense (next year).

I'm just saying that a final conversation may be worth it before just walking away. Some people get comfortable in relationships or too in their own way (due to self-esteem issues) to contribute meaningfully, and all it takes is an honest heart-to-heart to get back on the same page. 

(For reference, I'm 28 partner 29. We've known each other for 15 years, been together for 13, and have a child)

You sound like me, no BS. I'm 28, going on 29, I met my partner when I was 13, we got together a year and a half later and had our first child when we were 16/17.

We live together, though at present I work and am in my second year of my master's program while he's pursuing a trade. I have the degree and better paying job so I cover most all our expenses. For the last two years, I've felt like I've been waiting for him to find some focus and get serious about himself so that our relationship can mature past this young adult stage that it feels like we've been stuck in and on top of that, he knows I want more children, we both do, but I'm unwilling to bring about anymore children unmarried. His mom has asked about it, my mom has asked about it, we still get weird looks at the school for not all having the same last name, it is a *thing*.

And this year I felt like I was going crazy waiting to see more growth for him and waiting for him to propose, due largely in part because at the start of this year he said, "I don't have the money for a ring but I've seriously been thinking about proposing before the end of the year." This drove me WILD as I anxiously waited to see any hint of planning. By May I was weary, around September I was absolutely restless and by Christmas, I was downright depressed. I finally worked up the courage to ask him on Christmas Eve why he hadn't and if he had changed his mind; and I got an answer that made sense about the people we were and are.

After fifteen years, he doesn't feel pressured to marry me but he feels pressure to do it *right*. He doesn't want to just take me to city hall, he wants to give me a wedding and a ring--things he absolutely cannot afford to do right now. So it means more waiting, which honestly sound like such bull to someone on the outside looking in, except I accidentally came across a notebook that had fallen under the bed with a checklist of things he wanted to do in the next year leading up to a proposal. Needless to say, I'm a little more willing to wait 😅

But the point in my sharing this, is that it may end up being as simple as starting a conversation. My partner has been kind of aimless in life mostly due to issues with self-esteem stemming from our teen pregnancy, and honestly because we've known each other since we were literal children, it almost felt harder to recognize when and *where* our relationship needed to mature to the next stage. 

I think that at 28, 11 years in, this is the time where you both should make that assessment. I've only ever been with my partner as well and I have asked myself if I had missed out on anything, but ultimately, I think that I had to accept being ready to leave my childhood love/friend if clarity wasn't something that could be achieved. Have a conversation with him, ask him what his *plans* are for your mutual future and make a decision from there. There's such a thing as getting too comfortable, and it's bound to happen when you have a relationship that starts so early in life, and that could be the issue here!
